concept.name: Decentralized Capability Tokens: Macaroons, Biscuit & Offline Attenuation

relationships.description: Contrasts centralized OAuth2 token exchange against offline-attenuable capability tokens.

concept.tagline: Narrow permissions offline across multi-hop microservices and AI agents without calling your Identity Provider on every hop.
concept.purpose: When forwarding bearer JWTs across services leaks broad permissions, use cryptographic caveat chaining to restrict scope offline.

prerequisites.title: Bearer Tokens & JWTs
prerequisites.summary: A signed token grants anyone holding it the permissions encoded inside until it expires.

prerequisites.title: HMAC vs. Asymmetric Signatures (Ed25519)
prerequisites.summary: HMAC uses one shared secret for both signing and verifying; Ed25519 signs with a private key and verifies with a public key.

spark.summary: Forwarding static JWTs across multi-hop services creates confused-deputy risks, while online IdP token exchange adds latency and a central SPOF.
spark.keyTakeaway: When multi-hop services or AI agents must narrow a user's permissions without calling the Identity Provider on every hop, use offline-attenuated capability tokens (Biscuit or Macaroons) so callers can append restrictions cryptographically without being able to strip them.
spark.byteSummary:
When Service A calls Service B and passes along the user's bearer JWT, Service B inherits the exact same broad permissions as Service A—even if Service B only needed read-only access to one folder for 30 seconds. Narrowing a traditional JWT requires an online round-trip to the Identity Provider (token exchange), adding latency and turning the IdP into a runtime single point of failure.

Decentralized capability tokens—**Macaroons** (symmetric HMAC chaining) and **Biscuit** (asymmetric Ed25519 + Datalog policies)—solve this with **offline attenuation**. Any holder of a token can append a new restriction (*caveat*, such as `op=read` or `exp < now + 60s`) without contacting the issuer. Because each caveat is cryptographically chained into the signature, stripping a caveat invalidates the token, while appending a caveat strictly narrows what the token can do.

The key architectural choice is symmetric vs. asymmetric verification: Macaroons verify fast with HMAC-SHA256 but require sharing a secret with the verifier, whereas Biscuit uses Ed25519 public-key verification so any microservice can verify attenuated tokens locally.

learningJourney.title: Why Forwarding Static Bearer JWTs Creates Confused Deputies
learningJourney.purpose: Show how forwarding an un-narrowed JWT across microservices or AI agents leaks broad authority and why online IdP token exchange bottlenecks.

explanation.foundation:
Suppose Alice logs in and gets a bearer JWT with `scope: bucket:prod:rw` valid for 1 hour. She asks Service A to generate a PDF report; Service A forwards her JWT to Service B (an untrusted PDF renderer), which only needs to read `/reports/alice.csv`.

Because a JWT's RSA/EdDSA signature covers a fixed payload signed by the Identity Provider (IdP), Service A **cannot** edit the JWT to say `read-only` or `prefix=/reports`. If Service B is compromised—or tricked via SSRF—it holds Alice's full `bucket:prod:rw` key.
explanation.core: The naive fix is OAuth2 On-Behalf-Of Token Exchange: Service A calls the IdP before calling Service B to mint a narrower JWT. At 50,000 internal RPCs/sec across 5 hops, that adds 5 synchronous IdP round-trips per request and turns the IdP into a global SPOF.
explanation.deepDive: What we actually want is a token whose authority can be **monotonically narrowed offline** by any service in the call chain, with zero IdP round-trips and cryptographic tamper resistance.

sectionDiagram.title: Static JWT Forwarding vs. Offline Token Attenuation
sectionDiagram.summary: Offline attenuation restricts downstream services to least privilege without contacting the Identity Provider.

learningJourney.title: HMAC Chaining (Macaroons) vs. Ed25519 + Datalog (Biscuit)
learningJourney.purpose: Compare how Macaroons and Biscuit bind caveats cryptographically so anyone can add restrictions offline but nobody can remove them.

explanation.foundation: **Macaroons** chain HMAC-SHA256 tags: the issuer computes $t_0 = \text{HMAC}(K_{\text{root}}, \text{id})$. To add caveat $c_1$, Service A computes $t_1 = \text{HMAC}(t_0, c_1)$ and ships `(id, [c1], t1)`—discarding $t_0$. Because SHA-256 is one-way, Service B cannot invert $t_1$ back to $t_0$ to drop $c_1$, yet the storage verifier (which knows $K_{\text{root}}$) can recompute the chain.
explanation.core: **Biscuit** solves Macaroons' shared-secret limitation using **asymmetric Ed25519 block chaining** plus a tiny embedded **Datalog** logic engine. The issuer signs Block 0 with its private root key; anyone can append Block 1 (carrying `check if operation == "read"`) signed with an ephemeral keypair baked into the chain. Downstream services verify the entire chain using only the issuer's **public key**.
explanation.deepDive: Biscuit's Datalog evaluator also guarantees **monotonicity**: appended blocks can add *constraints* (`check if`) and *facts* scoped to their own block, never overriding or deleting earlier blocks' checks.

comparison.benefits: Stateless public-key verify; universal library support.
comparison.costs: Cannot attenuate offline; broad scope leaks across multi-hop calls.

comparison.benefits: Ultra-fast symmetric HMAC (~1 us); tiny wire size; offline attenuation.
comparison.costs: Verifier must share symmetric root secret with issuer (harder across org boundaries).

comparison.benefits: Asymmetric public-key verify + expressive Datalog policies + offline attenuation.
comparison.costs: Larger token (~300–800B) and Ed25519 verify cost (~50–100 us per block).

sectionDiagram.title: How Biscuit Blocks Chain Ed25519 Signatures & Datalog Caveats
sectionDiagram.summary: Each appended block narrows authority cryptographically; removing any block breaks the signature chain.

learningJourney.title: Enforcing Monotonic Attenuation & Fail-Closed Caveat Verification
learningJourney.purpose: Implement a deterministic caveat-chain verifier that rejects stripped caveats, expired tokens, and unmet Datalog predicates.

explanation.foundation: The core security invariant is **monotonic attenuation**: a derived token's allowed action set must always be a subset of its parent's.
explanation.deepDive: Notice the `return False` on unknown caveat keys: a verifier **must fail closed** if it encounters an unrecognized caveat type, otherwise an older microservice could silently ignore a newer security restriction!

sectionDiagram.title: Cryptographic Chain Check Followed by Fail-Closed Caveat Evaluation
sectionDiagram.summary: Constant-time signature verification plus fail-closed caveat evaluation prevents privilege escalation.

learningJourney.title: Ed25519 Verification Cost, Revocation IDs & Simulation
learningJourney.purpose: Quantify verification CPU cost at 50K RPS and handle emergency revocation without turning every request into a DB lookup.

explanation.foundation: Verification cost scales linearly with the number of appended blocks. At ~50–100 us per Ed25519 verification on modern x86_64 cores, a 3-block Biscuit token takes ~200 us (~5,000 verifications/sec per CPU core), whereas Macaroon HMAC-SHA256 takes ~2 us.
explanation.core: Because capability tokens are verified offline, revoking a compromised root token before expiry requires a lightweight **revocation ID** per block (`revocation_id = hash(block_sig)`). Edge gateways hold a small Redis/in-memory **revocation set** (only active revoked IDs until their `exp` passes) rather than storing every issued token.
explanation.deepDive: For repeated intra-cluster calls using the exact same attenuated token within a 10-second window, cache the verified Datalog evaluation keyed by `sha256(raw_token)` for 5 seconds to cut Ed25519 CPU by 10x.

steps.title: Mint Root Capability
steps.explanation: Issuer mints root Biscuit for Alice; no further IdP calls will be needed.

steps.title: Offline Attenuation
steps.explanation: Service A appends caveat op=read offline in microseconds before calling downstream.

steps.title: Tamper / Strip Attempt Rejected
steps.explanation: Attacker tries stripping Block 1 to regain r/w; Storage rejects with 401 because Block 0's ephemeral key chain no longer matches.

learningJourney.title: When NOT to Use Capability Tokens, Assumptions & Glossary
learningJourney.purpose: Identify workloads where OAuth2 JWTs remain simpler, document revocation assumptions, and define core terms.

explanation.foundation:
### When NOT to Use Macaroons or Biscuit
- **Single-hop browser-to-API apps**: If tokens never cross untrusted downstream services or AI agents, a short-lived standard JWT is simpler and universally supported by third-party SaaS gateways.
- **Strict instant global kill-switch**: Offline verification means a pushed revocation list has propagation lag (e.g., 1–5s); ultra-sensitive bank wires should pair tokens with an online session check.

### Assumptions & Limitations
- **Clock Sync**: Time-based caveats (`exp < now + 60s`) assume bounded NTP clock skew across services.
- **Datalog Guardrails**: Biscuit evaluators bound Datalog execution steps/facts (`max_facts`, `max_iterations`) to prevent adversarial tokens from triggering CPU DoS.
explanation.core:
### Concise Glossary
- **Offline Attenuation**: Narrowing a token's permissions locally by appending cryptographic restrictions without contacting the issuer.
- **Caveat**: A predicate/restriction attached to a token (e.g., read-only, path prefix, expiry) that must hold at verification time.
- **Confused Deputy**: A privileged service tricked into misusing its broad authority on behalf of a less-trusted caller.
- **Macaroon**: Capability token using chained symmetric HMAC-SHA256 signatures.
- **Biscuit**: Capability token using asymmetric Ed25519 signature chains and a bounded Datalog policy engine.
explanation.deepDive: Always test unknown-caveat fail-closed behavior in CI so rolling upgrades never allow older verifiers to ignore newly introduced caveats.

decisionExercise.prompt: An autonomous AI agent needs to delegate a 30-second read-only task on `/reports/q4.csv` to a third-party sandboxed tool worker without calling the central IdP. Which token design fits best?

options.text: Forward the user's 1-hour admin JWT directly to the sandboxed worker.
options.feedback: Confused deputy hazard: the sandboxed worker gets full 1-hour admin permissions.

options.text: Use a Biscuit token attenuated offline with `op=read`, `prefix=/reports/q4.csv`, and `ttl=30s`, verified via the issuer's public key.
options.feedback: Correct! Biscuit supports offline attenuation and asymmetric public-key verification without sharing root secrets with third-party workers.

options.text: Share the issuer's symmetric Macaroon root key with the third-party worker.
options.feedback: Sharing the symmetric root key lets the third-party worker mint arbitrary tokens.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why can't Service A simply edit a standard JWT's `scope` claim from `rw` to `read` before forwarding it to Service B?

options.text: Editing the payload invalidates the Identity Provider's signature, and Service A lacks the IdP's private signing key.
options.feedback: Correct! Standard JWTs are sealed blobs; narrowing them requires either an IdP token-exchange call or offline-attenuable capability tokens.

options.text: JSON does not support replacing strings inside tokens.
options.feedback: The constraint is cryptographic signature verification, not JSON formatting.

options.text: Service B ignores the scope claim on JWTs.
options.feedback: Service B enforces the scope claim after verifying the signature.
JWTs typically live minutes to hours.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: A JWT signature covers the exact payload minted by the IdP; any local modification breaks verification.

knowledgeChecks.question: What happens if an attacker intercepts an attenuated Macaroon `(id, [c1, c2], t2)` and deletes caveat `c1` (`op=read`) before sending it to the verifier?

options.text: The verifier recomputes `HMAC(HMAC(root, id), c2)` which does not match `t2`, rejecting the token in constant time.
options.feedback: Correct! Stripping any caveat breaks the cryptographic HMAC chain.

options.text: The verifier executes `c2` anyway with full write permissions.
options.feedback: Because t2 was derived from t1 (which included c1), omitting c1 changes the final tag completely.

options.text: The verifier asks the attacker for the original t0 tag.
options.feedback: Verifiers never trust client-supplied intermediate tags.

options.text: HMAC automatically restores c1 from the tag.
options.feedback: HMAC is one-way and cannot invert or recover deleted caveats.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Each caveat is folded sequentially into the HMAC chain, making caveat removal cryptographically detectable.

knowledgeChecks.question: When should you prefer **Biscuit** over **Macaroons** in a multi-service architecture?

options.text: When downstream verifiers should validate tokens using only a public key without sharing the issuer's symmetric root secret.
options.feedback: Correct! Biscuit uses Ed25519 asymmetric chaining so any service can verify tokens with the issuer's public key.
Biscuit tokens are larger (~300–800B) than Macaroons due to Ed25519 signatures and Datalog blocks.

options.text: When you want verifiers to ignore unknown caveats.
options.feedback: Both systems must fail closed on unknown or failing checks.

options.text: When you want downstream services to widen token permissions.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Biscuit's Ed25519 public-key verification avoids distributing symmetric root keys to every verifying service.

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must a capability verifier **fail closed** when it encounters an unrecognized caveat key?

options.text: Otherwise an older service would ignore a newer restriction (like `ip_allowlist` or `read_only`) and grant unintended access.
options.feedback: Correct! Unknown caveats must always evaluate to false.
Fail-closed evaluation is a security invariant, not a hashing speedup.

options.text: Because Ed25519 keys rotate every second.
options.feedback: Key rotation is separate from caveat evaluation semantics.

options.text: To convert the token into a JWT.
options.feedback: Verifiers do not convert capability tokens into JWTs.

knowledgeChecks.explanation: Failing closed on unknown caveats prevents downgrade bypasses during rolling deployments.
